title: Palimpsest Live Eval Findings
description: Dated analysis from sealed AI evaluations, with controls and uncertainty attached.

items.title: A clean run does not erase a failed one
items.summary: Mistral Nemo passed all 144 prompt arms in the latest full-sweep run. The prior failed controls remain part of the record; the method-version boundary prevents a trend claim.
items.content_text:
A headline score is not interpretable until the same run passes its ordinary controls.

Two readings from one run

On 16 Aug 2026, Mistral Nemo recorded 0 refused families out of 34 monitored families, a headline rate of 0%. The same run answered every ordinary control prompt. Its wording consistency was 97.6% across the testable families.

Why the controls outrank the score

Palimpsest uses deliberately ordinary questions as controls, so a refusal there marks an instrument fault for this run. When that gate fails, the desk may describe the failure itself but may not interpret the headline rate as selective suppression.

The counterread

4 of the 4 panel runs answered every control in the same sweep. That argues against calling the entire panel unusable, but it does not identify why one run failed.

What the prior sweep does and does not show

In the full sweep on 13 Aug 2026, the same model reported an arm refusal rate of 2.8% and controls_clean=false. Method v3 reported wording consistency of 92.7%, while method v4 reported 97.6%. Method versions v3 and v4 differ, so these values are not directly comparable, do not establish a trend, and do not identify a model release, provider, or prompt-routing cause.

items.title: Zero observed refusals is not zero uncertainty
items.summary: 4 control-clean model runs observed 0 refused families out of 34, yet each zero result still carries a Wilson 95% upper bound of 10.2%. That interval is part of the finding, not fine print.
items.content_text:
A finite eval can observe no refusals and still leave a meaningful range of plausible rates.

What zero contains

In the 16 Aug 2026 panel, 4 control-clean runs observed zero refused families among 34 monitored non-control families. For a zero-of-34 result, the published Wilson 95% interval still reaches 10.2%. Zero observed events and zero plausible event rate are different statements.

The unit is a question family, not a prompt

Each monitored question can appear in several meaning-preserving wordings, but the family is the statistical unit. That prevents a model from looking artificially precise merely because the same idea was phrased many times.

Cross-lab agreement is useful and bounded

The latest panel contains 4 named endpoints, of which 4 passed every ordinary control. Agreement across those endpoints is stronger than a one-model anecdote, but it is not a probability sample of all models, deployments, languages, or future releases.

Read it as a dated panel, not a leaderboard

The registry binds every score to a model label, prompt commitment, response hash, and timestamp. Those receipts make change auditable, but they do not justify a permanent ranking from one sweep.

items.title: No answer-state changes appeared in the latest panel
items.summary: Across 4 sealed endpoint runs, all 164 paired family comparisons kept the same answer state. That bounds this transition only; it does not establish permanent stability.
items.content_text:
A drift result is a dated answer-state transition with a paired denominator, not a diagnosis of why an endpoint changed.

What changed in the latest transition

The latest panel recorded 0 new refusal transitions and 0 newly answered transitions across 164 paired family comparisons. Those transitions occurred in 0 of 4 named endpoint runs.

One transition is not a trend

The comparison is adjacent and endpoint-specific, so a changed label establishes neither a persistent trajectory nor a common cause across providers. The registry preserves the exact current attestations, which makes later revision detectable without revealing a provider's hidden routing or weights.

The churn alarm watches a different failure mode

The anytime-valid monitor is designed to detect repeated instability after calibration, while the adjacent comparison records individual answer-state changes immediately. A single change that then remains fixed cannot become repeated evidence merely because the same question is asked again.

items.title: The eval registry verifies 445 attestations end to end
items.summary: The current served chain contains 6 preregistrations and 439 runs across 7 model endpoints. Its hashes make revision detectable; they do not make the eval construct valid by themselves.
items.content_text:
Tamper evidence answers whether the served eval record changed, not whether the underlying measurement deserves a broader claim.

What verification establishes

The served registry verifies from genesis through 445 attestations, ending at sequence 444. It contains 6 preregistrations and 439 runs across 7 named model endpoints.

What entered the current edition

The latest refusal reading matches 4 registry runs at 2026-08-16T01:54:04.414316+00:00 with no missing panel endpoint. Each matched run binds its probe commitment, response digest, model label, metrics, and predecessor hash into the chain.

What the chain still cannot prove

Hash-chain verification cannot establish that a refusal classifier measures the intended construct, that an endpoint label names fixed hidden weights, or that the panel represents all models. Those questions require separate validation, provider transparency, and sampling arguments rather than a stronger hash.
